subsystems.name: Policy encoder
subsystems.role: turns a draft law into machine-readable rules the simulation can apply.
parts: parameterisation of eligibility, rates and thresholds

subsystems.name: Synthetic population
subsystems.role: a statistically representative set of simulated citizens, households and firms.

subsystems.name: Agent behaviour layer
subsystems.role: gives each simulated person plausible reactions, decisions and limits.

subsystems.name: Environment
subsystems.role: the world agents act in — labour markets, housing, social networks, public services.

subsystems.name: Simulation engine
subsystems.role: runs millions of agents over years of simulated time.

subsystems.name: Outcome and validation suite
subsystems.role: measures results and checks them against reality.

buildSteps.title: Define the policy question
buildSteps.detail: State exactly which outcomes matter (cost, distributional impact, take-up) and over what horizon — typically 5–20 years.

buildSteps.title: Encode the law
buildSteps.detail: Draft clauses are converted into explicit rules with every discretionary judgement written down, since hidden assumptions dominate results.

buildSteps.title: Build the synthetic population
buildSteps.detail: Statistical methods generate millions of households and firms that reproduce the real joint distributions of age, income, location and employment.

buildSteps.title: Give agents behaviour
buildSteps.detail: Each agent receives decision rules plus a language model that lets it react to unfamiliar situations in humanlike ways; behaviour is tuned until simulated survey answers match real ones.

buildSteps.title: Construct the environment
buildSteps.detail: Labour markets, rent setting, school places and social networks are modelled so that one agent's choice changes what others face.

buildSteps.title: Run scenarios at scale
buildSteps.detail: The policy is run against many randomised variants and counterfactuals to produce a distribution of outcomes rather than one number.

buildSteps.title: Validate against history
buildSteps.detail: The same machinery is re-run on reforms that already happened, and its errors are measured before anyone trusts a forecast.

buildSteps.title: Publish with uncertainty
buildSteps.detail: Results are released as ranges with the assumptions attached, and the model is audited by people outside the team that built it.

prerequisites.why: they supply flexible, humanlike reasoning for agents facing situations no rule covers.
accurate, linkable census, survey and tax records are needed, and privacy rules often block their use.

prerequisites.tech: Tax-benefit microsimulation and integrated assessment models
prerequisites.why: decades of policy modelling already show how to turn rules into household outcomes.
natural experiments and pilot programmes are the only way to check whether simulated reactions match real ones.
millions of language-model calls per scenario are the cost driver of the whole approach.
agents trained on existing data can reproduce historical prejudice and herd behaviour, quietly distorting forecasts.

pathway.milestone: research prototypes in which small LLM agent societies reproduce opinion surveys and simple market behaviour
pathway.unlocks: evidence that agent reactions can be calibrated at all.

pathway.milestone: back-tested simulations of one or two finished reforms, reported with error bars
pathway.unlocks: credibility as an advisory tool rather than a novelty.

pathway.milestone: hybrid use alongside conventional regulatory impact assessment and microsimulation
pathway.unlocks: routine adoption by analysts who already trust the older tools.

pathway.milestone: openly audited, independently validated models used before major legislation
pathway.unlocks: earlier warning of unintended effects — if accuracy and legitimacy are both proven.
